source_text: Quod adtinet ad bonitatis quaestionem, his lineis deduximus eam minime deo adaequare, ut neque ingenitam neque rationalem neque perfectam, sed et improbam et iniustam et ipso iam bonitatis nomine indignam, quod scilicet in quantum deo congruat, in tantum deum non esse conueniat qui de tali bonitate etiam praeferatur, nec de tali modo uerum et sola. iam enim et hoc discuti par est, an deus de sola bonitate censendus sit, negatis ceteris adpendicibus sensibus et adfectibus. quos Marcionitae quidem a deo suo abigunt in creatorem. nos uero [et] agnoscimus in creatore ut deo dignos, et ex hoc quoque negabimus deum in quo non omnia, quae deo digna sint, constent. si aliquem de Epicuri schola deum adfectauit Christi nomine titulare, ut quod beatum et incorruptibile sit neque sibi neque alii molestias praestet — hanc enim sententiam ruminans Marcion remouit ab illo seueritates et iudiciarias uires —: aut in totum inmobilem et stupentem deum concepisse debuerat — et quid illi cum Christo, molesto et Iudaeis per doctrinam et sibi per Iesum? — aut et de ceteris motibus eum agnouisse. — et quid illi cum Epicuro, nec sibi nec Christianis necessario? ecce enim hoc ipso, quod retro quietus, qui nec notitiam sui aliquo interim opere curauerit, post tantum aeui senserit in hominis salutem, utique per uoluntatem, nonne concussibilis tunc fuit nouae uoluntati, ut et ceteris motibus uideatur obnoxius? quae enim uoluntas sine concupiscentiae stimulo est? [quis uolet quod non concupiscet?] sed et cura accedet uoluntati. quis enim uolet quid et concupiscet, et non curabit? igitur cum et uoluit et concupiit in hominis salutem, iam et sibi et aliis negotium fecit, Epicuro nolente, consiliario Marcionis. nam et aduersarium sibi constituit: ipsum illud, aduersus quod et uoluit et concupiit et curauit, siue delictum siue mortem. inprimis ipsum arbitrum eorum et dominum hominis, creatorem. porro nihil sine aemulatione decurret, quod sine aduersario non erit. denique uolens et concupiscens et curans hominem liberare, hoc ipso iam aemulatur et eum, a quo liberat, aduersus eum scilicet sibi liberaturus, et ea, de quibus liberat, in alia liberaturus. proinde autem aemulationi occurrant necesse est officiales suae in ea, quae aemulatur: ira discordia odium dedignatio indignatio bilis nolentia offensa. haec omnia si aemulationi adsistunt, aemulatio autem liberando homini procurat, liberatio autem hominis operatio bonitatis est, non poterit ea bonitas sine suis dotibus, id est sine sensibus et adfectibus, per quos administratur aduersus creatorem, ne sic quoque inrationalis praescribatur, si careat et sensibus et adfectibus debitis. haec multo plenius defendemus in causa creatoris, in qua et exprobrantur.
pass_a_gloss: As for the question of goodness, we have led it down these lines, that it is not at all equal to God, so that it is not innate, nor rational, nor perfect, but also wicked and unjust and unworthy of the very name of goodness, because, of course, insofar as it is fitting for God, to that extent it is not suitable for God to be, who is even preferred for such goodness, nor true and alone in such a way. For now, it is also fitting to discuss whether God should be considered as being of sole goodness, with the other appendages of senses and affections denied. Which the Marcionites, indeed, drive away from their God to the Creator. But we, on the other hand, recognize in the Creator, as being worthy of God, and from this also, we will deny that God, in whom not all things, which are worthy of God, are present. If someone from the school of Epicurus has attempted to title a God with the name of Christ, so that, because he is blessed and incorruptible, he does not provide troubles for himself or for another — for Marcion, ruminating on this opinion, removed the severities and judicial powers from him —: either he ought to have conceived of a completely immobile and stunned God — and what does he have to do with Christ, who is troublesome to the Jews through doctrine and to himself through Jesus? — or he ought to have recognized him also from the other motions. — And what does he have to do with Epicurus, neither necessarily for himself nor for the Christians? Behold, for in this very thing, that he, who was quiet previously, who did not take care of the knowledge of himself by any work in the meantime, has perceived, after so great a age, the salvation of man, undoubtedly through will, was he not moved by a new will, so that he seems to be subject also to the other motions? For what will is without the stimulus of desire? [Who wills what he does not desire?] But also care will be added to the will. For who wills and desires something and does not take care? Therefore, when he both willed and desired the salvation of man, he has already made trouble for himself and for others, against the will of Epicurus, the advisor of Marcion. For he has also set up an adversary for himself: that very thing, against which he willed and desired and took care, whether it be sin or death. First and foremost, the very judge and lord of men, the Creator. Furthermore, nothing will run its course without emulation, which will not be without an adversary. Finally, willing and desiring and taking care to liberate man, he is already emulating and that one, from whom he liberates, against whom, of course, he will liberate himself, and those things, from which he liberates, he will liberate into other things. Therefore, it is necessary that the officials of emulation, namely, anger, discord, hatred, disdain, indignation, bile, unwillingness, offense, occur in that which is emulated. All these things, if they assist emulation, and emulation, in liberating man, procures, and the liberation of man is an operation of goodness, that goodness will not be able to be without its endowments, that is, without the senses and affections, through which it is administered against the Creator, lest it be prescribed as irrational, if it lacks the senses and affections that are due. We will defend these things much more fully in the case of the Creator, in which also the reproaches are.
pass_b_english: On the question of goodness, we have traced the argument this far: Marcion's 'goodness' does not measure up to God at all. It is neither innate, nor rational, nor perfect; it is wicked, unjust, and unworthy of the very name of goodness. The logic is inescapable: to the degree this 'goodness' suits God, it disqualifies Him from being God, since He is exalted on the strength of such a counterfeit goodness, and cannot be true or unique in that mode. This forces the further question: should God be defined by goodness alone, once senses and affections — those so-called 'appendages' — are stripped away? The Marcionites shunt those faculties off their God and dump them on the Creator. We, by contrast, recognize those same faculties in the Creator as worthy of God, and on that ground we refuse to call any being 'God' if it lacks the full complement of divine attributes. Suppose some Epicurean tries to baptize a god with the name of Christ, picturing a blessed, incorruptible being who causes no trouble to himself or anyone else — Marcion chewed over this very view and stripped his god of severity and judicial power. He had only two options: conceive a completely inert, stunned deity — but then what has that god to do with Christ, who is an offense to Jews by His teaching and to Marcion by His Jesus? — or admit that God possesses the full range of motion. But then what has he to do with Epicurus, who is necessary to neither him nor Christians? Look at the dilemma: this god, previously at rest, indifferent to making himself known by any act for eons, suddenly takes notice of human salvation. That shift can only come by an act of will. Was he not, then, shaken by a new will, proving himself subject to every other motion as well? What is a will without the goad of desire? [Who wills what he does not desire?] And desire inevitably drags care in its wake: who wills and desires a thing, yet takes no trouble for it? So once this god both willed and desired man's salvation, he created trouble for himself and others, Epicurus — Marcion's adviser — notwithstanding. He manufactured an adversary: the very thing he opposed by willing, desiring, and striving, whether sin or death. First and foremost, that adversary is the Judge and Lord of men, the Creator. Moreover, no contest runs its course without rivalry, and rivalry cannot exist without an opponent. Thus, by willing, desiring, and striving to liberate man, this god is already locked in rivalry — with the one from whom he liberates, against whom he must liberate himself, and with the things from which he liberates, into which he must liberate them. Consequently, the attendants of rivalry — anger, discord, hatred, contempt, indignation, bile, unwillingness, offense — must show up in the very arena where he rivals. If rivalry brings these in its train, and rivalry, by liberating man, achieves the work of goodness, then that goodness cannot exist without its own endowments — that is, without the senses and affections through which it operates against the Creator — lest it be exposed as irrational for lacking the very faculties it owes. We will defend all this far more fully in the case for the Creator, where these charges are also answered.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological argument regarding the necessity of divine affections (senses and emotions) to avoid an irrational or inert deity. Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a fluent, idiomatic rendering that preserves all nuances of the Latin text, including the rhetorical questions and the specific list of 'officials' of emulation. All clauses, including the parenthetical question [quis uolet quod non concupiscet?], are correctly handled.
